DIRECTIONS FOR USE (Refer to diagram for reference)
1. Attach a rotating hemostatic valve (RHV) to the guidewire lumen of the balloon catheter. Set up a
continuous saline flush line and connect it to the sidearm of the RHV.
2. Choose appropriate guiding or diagnostic catheter. Attach a RHV to the proximal hub of the guiding or
diagnostic catheter. To prevent backflow of blood into the lumen of the catheter, connect the continuous
saline flush line to the sidearm of the RHV.
3. Open the RHV on the hub of the guiding or diagnostic catheter and introduce the balloon
catheter/guidewire into the guiding catheter using the introducer sheath. Carefully advance the balloon
catheter/guidewire to the guiding catheter distal tip. After the balloon catheter/guidewire reaches the tip of
the guiding catheter, remove the introducer from the balloon catheter shaft by retracting the introducer
from the RHV and peeling off the introducer. Advance the balloon catheter through the RHV.
4. Advance the balloon catheter and guidewire to the desired location in the vasculature using fluoroscopic
visualization. Carefully tighten the valve of the RHV around the balloon catheter to prevent leakage from
the RHV. The RHV should still allow for balloon catheter advancement after tightening.
WARNING: Do not over-tighten the RHV around the balloon catheter. Over-tightening could delay balloon
inflation and deflation.
WARNING: Do not advance the balloon catheter or guidewire against resistance. If resistance is felt,
assess the source of resistance using fluoroscopic means.
5. Attach a 2-way stopcock to a 1cc syringe filled with appropriate contrast solution. Prime the 2-way
stopcock so that no air is present.

DEVICE DESCRIPTION
The SOFIA Catheter is a non-tapered, single-lumen, flexible catheter equipped with the coil and the braid
reinforcement. The distal segment is steam-shapeable to facilitate vessel selection and also has a hydrophilic
coating for navigation through the vasculatures. The radiopaque marker is located at the distal end of the catheter
for visualization under fluoroscopy.
CONTENTS
One Catheter
One Introducer Sheath
One Shaping Mandrel
INDICATIONS FOR USE/INTENDED PURPOSE
The SOFIA Catheter is indicated for general intravascular use, including the neuro and peripheral vasculature. The
SOFIA Catheter can be used to facilitate introduction of diagnostic or therapeutic agents. The SOFIA Catheter is
not intended for use in coronary arteries. Moreover, the SOFIA Catheter is intended for use in removal/aspiration of
emboli and thrombi from selected blood vessels in the arterial system, including the peripheral and neuro
vasculatures.
CONTRAINDICATIONS
There are no known contraindications.

DEVICE DESCRIPTION
The SOFIA 88 Catheter is a non-tapered, single-lumen, flexible catheter equipped with coil and braid
reinforcement. The distal segment is designed to facilitate vessel selection with 60 cm of distal-shaft
hydrophilic coating for navigation through the vasculature. The radiopaque marker is located at the distal end of
the catheter for visualization under fluoroscopy.

INDICATIONS FOR USE
The SOFIA 88 Catheter is indicated for general intravascular use, including the neuro and peripheral vasculature.
The SOFIA 88 Catheter can be used to facilitate introduction of diagnostic agents or therapeutic devices. The
SOFIA 88 Catheter is not intended for use in coronary arteries.
CONTRAINDICATIONS
There are no known contraindications.

POTENTIAL COMPLICATIONS
Potential complications include but are not limited to: vessel or aneurysm perforation, vasospasm, hematoma at
the site of entry, embolism, ischemia, intracerebral/intracranial hemorrhage, pseudo aneurysm, seizure, stroke,
infection, vessel dissection, thrombus formation, and death.
Potential complications related to angiographic and fluoroscopic X-ray radiation doses include, but are not
limited to, alopecia, burns ranging in severity from skin reddening to ulcers, cataracts, and delayed neoplasia.
The probability of occurrence of complications may increase as procedure time and number of procedures
increase.

PRÉCAUTIONS
Le cathéter SOFIA 88 doit être manipulé avec précaution, afin de réduire les risques de dommages accidentels.
Vérifier la compatibilité du cathéter SOFIA 88 avec d’autres dispositifs auxiliaires couramment utilisés dans les
procédures intravasculaires. Le médecin doit bien connaître les techniques percutanées et intravasculaires et
les complications possibles associées à la procédure.
Il convient de faire preuve de prudence lors de la manipulation du cathéter SOFIA 88 dans les vaisseaux
tortueux, afin d’éviter de les endommager. Éviter d’avancer ou de retirer le dispositif face à une résistance
jusqu’à ce que la cause de la résistance soit déterminée.
La présence de calcifications, d’irrégularités ou d’autres dispositifs peut endommager le cathéter SOFIA 88
et potentiellement affecter son insertion ou son retrait.
Maintenir la perfusion de sérum physiologique hépariné dans la lumière interne du cathéter SOFIA 88 afin
d’éviter la formation de thrombus.
S’il est retiré du patient, le cathéter SOFIA 88 avec revêtement hydrophile doit être hydraté à l’aide d’une

COMPLICATIONS POTENTIELLES
Les complications potentielles comprennent, sans s’y limiter, la perforation d’un vaisseau ou d’un anévrisme,
le vasospasme, l’hématome au point d’entrée, l’embolie, l’ischémie, l’hémorragie intracérébrale/intracrânienne,
le pseudo-anévrisme, la crise d’épilepsie, l’accident vasculaire cérébral, l’infection, la dissection du vaisseau,
la formation d’un thrombus et la mort.
Les complications potentielles liées aux doses de radiations angiographiques et fluoroscopiques comprennent, entre
autres, l’alopécie, les brûlures allant du rougissement de la peau aux ulcères, la cataracte et la néoplasie tardive.
La probabilité de survenue de complications augmente avec la durée de l’intervention et le nombre d’interventions.

Potential complications include, but are not limited to: vessel or aneurysm perforation, vasospasm,
hematoma at the site of entry, embolism, ischemia, intracerebral/intracranial hemorrhage, pseudo
aneurysm, seizure, stroke, infection, vessel dissection, thrombus formation, and death.
SOFIA EX Catheters (IFU100157X2)
Potential complications include but are not limited to: vessel or aneurysm perforation, vasospasm,
hematoma at the site of entry, embolism, ischemia, intracerebral/intracranial hemorrhage, pseudo
aneurysm, seizure, stroke, infection, vessel dissection, thrombus formation, and death.
Potential X-ray radiation exposure related adverse events include but are not limited to: alopecia,
burns ranging in severity from skin reddening to ulcers, cataracts, delayed neoplasia, tissue
necrosis, and risks associated with contrast dye.

1.5.2 Clinical Performance and Safety
The devices within the SOFIA Catheter Family may be used as access devices to support and
advance a primary treatment device to the target vascular anatomy. Thus, clinical outcomes from
procedures in which the SOFIA catheters are in this way are generally difficult to directly attribute

1.6.2 Thrombolytic Drugs
Treatment options for AIS include intravenous thrombolysis (IVT) using recombined tissue
plasminogen activator (tPA) such as alteplase or tenecteplase, or intra-arterial (IA) thrombolysis
using urokinase22-26. IVT has been reported to be effective in improving functional outcomes after
ischemic stroke up to 4.5-9 hours after symptom onset The US Food and Drug Administration
(FDA) has only approved alteplase for use within 3 hours of stroke onset, but regulatory agencies
in most other countries, including those in the European Union, have approved its administration
within 4.5 hours of stroke onset.20 The FDA approval was based upon the results of the 1995
National Institute of Neurological Disorders and Stroke (NINDS) tPA trial. This trial was able to
show a significant improvement in functional outcome at 90 days when tPA was given 3 hours of
symptom onset. The European Cooperative Acute Stroke Studies (ECASS-III) evaluating the

1.6.3 Endovascular treatment
Although IV-tPA has been shown to be effective, its effectiveness may diminish with more
proximal or larger occlusions. The low success of tPA to achieve recanalization of LVO prompted
development of endovascular treatment. This was possible due to technological advances in
endovascular surgery with better catheters to enable more distal access and better stent retrievers
to safely remove the thrombi from brain vessels. The benefit of endovascular mechanical
thrombectomy (EMT) for AIS caused by emergent LVO in the anterior circulation has been
uniformly reported by RCT and meta-analyses up to 24 hours after last known well.23,24,30,32 In
mechanical thrombectomy, devices that remove blood clots from a large cerebral artery and to
restore blood flow comprise mostly 2 types: stent retrievers and aspiration catheters.33 Those

1.6.3.2 Aspiration
Despite the positive results of the stent retrievers with successful recanalization, there are some
vessel occlusions and thrombi that are resistant to this technique even after repeated recanalization
attempts. These vessel occlusions include cases of terminal ICA occlusions. Moreover “hard”
thrombi in other locations, such as the MCA, can also been resistant to the stent retriever technique.
For these cases, direct aspiration of the thrombus can be used as an alternative technique.37
Mechanical thrombectomy with aspiration, uses large bore aspiration catheters guided to the
proximal end of the clot put under negative pressure using an electric pump or manual suction with
a syringe to retrieve the clot (the thrombus is either aspirated through the catheter or stuck at the
tip and retrieved with the aspiration catheter).33 During aspiration thrombectomy, aspiration
catheters are placed through a guide catheter and advanced coaxially over a microcatheter or
microwire to the occluded vessel. The microcatheter or microwire is advanced through the clot,
and the aspiration catheter is advanced into the proximal clot.

The Headway™ and Wedge™ Microcatheters are available in seven types:
Device Headway 17 Advanced Soft, Headway 17 Advanced, Headway 21, Headway
27, Headway Duo, and Wedge and Wedge XL Microcatheters. In this
document, the five Headway™ Microcatheters will be grouped together and
referred to as “Headway” and the two Wedge™ Microcatheters will be grouped
together and referred to as “Wedge,” unless noted otherwise.
The Headway Microcatheters are single lumen catheter designed to be
introduced over a steerable guidewire to access small, tortuous vasculature.
The semi-rigid proximal section transitions to a flexible distal tip to facilitate
advancement through vessels. Dual radiopaque markers at the distal end

The Wedge Microcatheters are single lumen catheter designed to be introduced
over a steerable guidewire to access small, tortuous vasculature. The semi-
rigid proximal section transitions to a flexible distal tip to facilitate
advancement through vessels. Radiopaque markers at the distal end facilitate
fluoroscopic visualization. A larger diameter distal segment helps provide
stability for navigation. The outer surface of the Wedge Microcatheter is coated
with a hydrophilic polymer to increase lubricity; the distal 110 cm outer surface
of the Wedge XL Microcatheter is coated with a hydrophilic polymer to
increase lubricity. A luer fitting on the Wedge Microcatheter hub is used for
the attachment of accessories.
Design Characteristics The principle of operation of the Headway™ and Wedge™ Microcatheters
of the Device incorporates various design features that allow it to achieve its intended use. A
semi-rigid proximal section allows for steerability. Progressively softer
durometer distal segments and flexible tip allow for atraumatic navigation
through the vasculature.

durometer distal segments and flexible tip allow for atraumatic navigation
through the vasculature. Radiopaque markers allow for fluoroscopic
visualization. Hydrophilic polymer coating reduces friction during navigation
through the vasculature. A luer fitting on the hub allows for the attachment of
accessories. The hub/strain relief provides for kink resistance. Shapeable tip
allows the physician to form the optimal shape. The Wedge™ Microcatheter
includes an enlarged distal segment that allows for easier navigation through
certain parts of the vasculature, such as bifurcations, where a "ledge effect"
could occur.
Patient contact occurs with the catheter body and coating. The Headway™ and
Wedge™ Microcatheters do not incorporate a medicinal substance, animal
tissues or blood products.

1.4.3. Potential Complications / Adverse Effects
The potential complications / adverse effects for the Headway™ and Wedge™ Microcatheters
include, but are not limited to:
• vessel or aneurysm perforation
• vasospasm
• hematoma at the site of entry
• embolism
• ischemia
• intracerebral/intracranial hemorrhage
• pseudoaneurysm
• seizure
• stroke
• infection
• vessel dissection
• thrombus formation
• death

1.5.2. Clinical Performance and Safety
Neurovascular lesions, such as intracranial aneurysms, can cause potential injury or death if left
untreated. Endovascular interventions to treat these conditions require access to the desired
vascular site of treatment using access devices, including microcatheters. The Headway™ and
Wedge™ Microcatheters are intended for the introduction of interventional devices and infusion
of diagnostic agents into the neuro and peripheral vasculature, and as such, allows access to the
vascular site of interest.
Successful treatment of conditions avoids some risks and complications associated with these
conditions. Either the Headway™ or Wedge™ Microcatheters used as an access device is not a
primary therapeutic device on which the treatment outcomes of safety can be based. However,

In cases where lifestyle modification alone is not successful in reducing symptoms or progression
of the disease, the use of medication in conjunction with lifestyle modification may be
recommended. Statin therapy is by far the most well-recognized cholesterol-lowering therapy in
the management of cardiovascular and peripheral vascular disease. Other medical management
includes antiplatelet therapy, anticoagulation, vasodilators and antihypertensive therapy.
Treatment for thrombosis / embolisms, can include thrombolytic drugs, such as intravenous tissue
plasminogen activator (t-PA), however, intravenous thrombolysis can have limited reperfusion in
some anatomic locations as well as having a narrow therapeutic window (for example, ≤4.5 h after
onset in acute ischemic stroke (AIS)).
Open or laparoscopic surgery are more direct treatment options that can be used to ligate ruptured
blood vessels or malformations. The risk for open surgery includes restenosis, infection, and long
recovery time. If a patient is a candidate for either open or laparoscopic surgery, the less invasive
option is the current standard of care.
Endovascular surgery is a minimally invasive surgical option that delivers interventional therapies
for vascular disease from within the vascular system. Endovascular surgery can be used to either
inhibit or restore blood flow in the target vessels through the use of devices such as coils, stents,
stent retrievers (stentrievers) and flow diverters.

m. Endovascular surgery can be used to either
inhibit or restore blood flow in the target vessels through the use of devices such as coils, stents,
stent retrievers (stentrievers) and flow diverters. In treatment of AIS, endovascular mechanical
thrombectomy techniques combined with chemical thrombolysis are routinely utilized.
Endovascular surgery is initiated with the placement of a catheter through a major vessel (e.g.,
femoral or radial artery), passing from an entry incision site in the skin to the target vasculature.
Interventional therapies can then be delivered through the catheter. The placement of the catheter
requires the use of the Seldinger Technique. This technique involves an initial puncture of the
artery with a hollow needle, followed by the introduction of a guidewire through the needle. The
needle is then removed, and a catheter is tracked over the guidewire into the lumen of the vessel.
The guidewire can then be subsequently removed.
In endovascular procedures, both guide catheters and microcatheters, such as the subject devices
of this clinical evaluation, are used to advance interventional and diagnostic devices (e.g.,
guidewires, microcatheters, coils, stents, balloons, or chemical agents), through the vasculature
from the entry site to or nearly to the surgical location. Guide catheters are large diameter catheters
(5-7F) that provide support and lubricity for the passage of additional devices, sometimes
accommodating multiple devices simultaneously, through vascular anatomy. In contrast, the small
diameter of a microcatheter (1-3F) together with its steerability, trackability, and flexibility, allows
for navigation through narrow tortuous vessels for the distal placement of balloons, flow diverters,
coil, and other embolic or diagnostic agent.

2.6. Possible Diagnostic or Therapeutic Alternatives
When considering alternative treatments, it is recommended to contact your healthcare
professional who can take into account your individual situation.
Treatment option for blood vessel disease varies widely. Treatments can include treatments with
drugs or with surgery. A procedure that enters through a blood vessel is less involved than brain
surgery, for example.
A procedure that enters through a blood vessel involves using a special tool needed to make an
entry incision along a major blood vessel through which a flexible tube (catheter) can be placed
extending from the entry site to the target location within the blood vessel. Treatments or other
devices can then be delivered through the tube. The use of these flexible tubes is necessary for the
delivery of the medicine or other treatment device to the area where treatment is needed.
Catheters for this type of treatment are made by a number of companies. Please discuss with your
healthcare provider options for different devices.
2.7. Suggested Training for Users
The device should only be used by physicians who are familiar with use of catheters in blood
vessels in the head and body.

This system includes guide catheters and selective catheters engineered to reduce friction and enable reliable access through the radial artery pathway, which is an alternative to traditional femoral artery access.

Press Release Content: Balt Squid Liquid Embolic FDA PMA Approval STEM Trial - Balt, Inc. received FDA Premarket Approval (PMA) for Squid liquid embolic agent on February 4, 2026. Indicated for embolization of the middle meningeal artery (MMA) as an adjunct to usual care treatment in patients with symptomatic chronic subdural hematoma(s) measuring 10 mm or greater in thickness. The STEM trial (Squid Trial for the Embolization of the Middle Meningeal Artery) was the first prospective, randomized study assessing the impact of embolization on treatment failures in this patient population. STEM was a prospective, multi-center, international randomized controlled trial enrolling 310 patients comparing those who received embolization of the MMA with Squid Liquid Embolic as an adjunct to standard surgical or medical management against those who did not. Published in New England Journal of Medicine in November 2024, the study demonstrated that adjunctive embolization significantly reduced treatment failure rates without increasing adverse events. Primary outcome: 19 of 120 patients (16%) in the embolization group versus 47 of 129 patients (36%) in the control group, corresponding to a 64% relative reduction in risk. Squid is an ethyl vinyl alcohol (EVOH) copolymer-based device available in three viscosities (12, 18, and 34) with micronized tantalum. Originally approved in Europe in 2012. Pascal Girin, Balt CEO, noted this represents the company's first PMA approval and a major milestone. Press Release Content: EmboTrap II Early Postmarket Results Mechanical Thrombectomy AJNR 2021 - Published in American Journal of Neuroradiology (AJNR), May 2021, Volume 42, Issue 5, Pages 904-909. Title: 'Early Postmarket Results with EmboTrap II Stent Retriever for Mechanical Thrombectomy: A Multicenter Experience'. The EmboTrap II is a novel stent retriever with a dual-layer design and distal mesh. Study included seventy patients (mean age 69.9 years; 48.6% women) with emergent large-vessel occlusions in the ICA (n=18), M1 (n=38), M2 or M3 (n=13), and basilar artery (n=1). Key results: TICI 2b recanalization achieved in 95.7% overall (82.3% in EmboTrap II-only cases), first-pass efficacy achieved in 35.7%. Definitive treatment with alternative device required in 12.9% of cases. Hemorrhagic conversion noted in 22.9% (4.3% symptomatic). Conclusion: Initial postmarket results with EmboTrap II are favorable and comparable with other commercially available stent retrievers. This represents the first postmarket prospective multicenter experience following FDA approval. Press Release Content: EXCELLENT Registry EmboTrap endovascular stroke treatment Stroke journal 2024 - The EXCELLENT Registry is a prospective, multicenter, global registry of patients with acute ischemic stroke treated with EMBOTRAP as first-line mechanical thrombectomy device. Conducted at 34 sites (25 sites contributing clot) from September 2018 to March 2021. Registry utilized core imaging and central histology laboratories blinded to clinical data, independent 90-day modified Rankin Scale assessment, and Clinical Events Committee review. After screening 3799 patients, 997 subjects were included (mean age 70.0 ± 14.2 years; 51.8% women; 19.7% non-White). Key results: First-pass mTICI ≥2b rate was 64.5% (623/966), first-pass mTICI ≥2c was 39.1% (378/966), final mTICI ≥2b was 94.5% (931/985). Good clinical outcomes (mRS 0-2 or no worsening from baseline) noted in 46.8%, average NIHSS decrease 6.4 ± 7.9 points. Symptomatic intracranial hemorrhage rate 1.6%, all-cause mortality 19.1%. Published in Stroke journal in 2024. Press Release Content: EXTEND-IA Trial Published in NEJM 2015. The EXTEND-IA trial was published on February 11, 2015, in the New England Journal of Medicine. The trial tested the hypothesis that patients with anterior circulation ischemic stroke selected with evidence of vessel occlusion and salvageable tissue on perfusion imaging within 4.5 hours would have improved reperfusion and early neurologic improvement when treated with early endovascular thrombectomy using the Solitaire FR stent retriever after intravenous administration of alteplase, compared with alteplase alone. Study design: Patients receiving 0.9 mg of alteplase per kilogram of body weight less than 4.5 hours after stroke onset were randomly assigned to undergo endovascular thrombectomy with the Solitaire FR stent retriever or continue receiving alteplase alone. All patients had occlusion of the internal carotid or middle cerebral artery with salvageable brain tissue and ischemic core of less than 70 ml on CT perfusion imaging. Key results: Endovascular therapy, initiated at a median of 210 minutes after stroke onset, increased early neurologic improvement at 3 days (80% vs. 37%, P=0.002) and improved functional outcome at 90 days, with more patients achieving functional independence (71% vs. 40%; P=0.01). There were no significant differences in rates of death or symptomatic intracerebral hemorrhage. The trial was stopped early after 70 patients had undergone randomization (35 patients in each group). The release of the MR CLEAN trial results prompted the data and safety monitoring board to review the data, and the trial was stopped early because efficacy was clearly shown.

Press Release Content: HERMES Trial: Meta-Analysis of Endovascular Thrombectomy. Study Overview: The HERMES collaboration pooled individual patient data from five randomized trials (MR CLEAN, ESCAPE, REVASCAT, SWIFT PRIME, and EXTEND IA) conducted between December 2010 and December 2014. Patient Population: The analysis examined 1,287 patients—634 received endovascular thrombectomy, 653 received standard care—all with acute ischemic stroke from proximal anterior circulation vessel occlusion. Primary Clinical Result: Treatment with endovascular thrombectomy demonstrated substantial benefit with adjusted cOR 2.49, 95% CI 1.76-3.53; p<0.0001 for reduced disability at 90 days. The number needed to treat was 2.6 to prevent one additional patient from experiencing disability progression. Key Subgroup Findings: The intervention proved effective across diverse populations including patients aged 80+ years (cOR 3.68), benefit persisted when treatment occurred beyond 300 minutes post-symptom (cOR 1.76), and those ineligible for intravenous alteplase still benefited (cOR 2.43). Safety Profile: Mortality at 90 days and risk of parenchymal haematoma and symptomatic intracranial haemorrhage did not differ between populations. Clinical Significance: Results demonstrated no heterogeneity of treatment effect across subgroups, establishing endovascular thrombectomy as beneficial for most patients with this stroke type, regardless of demographics or geography.

Press Release Content: SEER Meta-Analysis: Solitaire Stent Retriever Functional Outcomes. The SEER (Safety and Efficacy of Solitaire Stent Thrombectomy) meta-analysis examined data from 787 patients across four randomized trials presented at the 2016 International Stroke Conference. Primary outcomes: Patients treated with Solitaire stent retriever plus IV-tPA demonstrated significantly better functional outcomes compared to IV-tPA alone with 54% vs 31.5%; P<.0001. The number needed to treat was remarkably low at 2.5, meaning approximately one patient per 2.5 treated showed improved functional results. For patients over 80 years old, the analysis revealed a substantial mortality reduction of 20% vs 40%; adjusted odds ratio, 3.7 (1.3–10.6); P=.01. Research indicated a time-dependent relationship, with outcomes declining as time from symptom onset to treatment increased. The device showed extremely low complication rates and low symptomatic intracranial hemorrhage. The meta-analysis synthesized results from SWIFT PRIME, REVASCAT, EXTEND-IA, and ESCAPE—all published in the New England Journal of Medicine in 2015.

Intended Use: The system targets patients with acute ischaemic stroke secondary to intracranial large vessel occlusive disease within eight hours of symptom onset, particularly useful for those ineligible for or unresponsive to intravenous tissue plasminogen activator (IV t-PA) therapy. Device Components: The Riptide platform consists of the Arc catheter, aspiration tubing, aspiration pump, and collection canister with intermediate tubing. Clinical Application: The device retrieves blood clots to restore blood flow in stroke patients. Interventional neuroradiologist Daniel Sahlein noted he would use it when treating stroke patients, particularly for basilar artery cases and selected anterior circulation situations.

Press Release Content: SWIFT Trial: Key Findings. Trial Overview: The SWIFT trial was a randomized, non-inferiority study comparing the Solitaire Flow Restoration Device against the Merci Retrieval System for treating acute ischemic stroke. Between February 2010 and February 2011, researchers enrolled 58 patients in the Solitaire group and 55 in the Merci group across 18 sites. Primary Efficacy Outcomes: The Solitaire device demonstrated superior performance on the primary endpoint with 61% vs 24% achieving proper blood flow restoration without symptomatic bleeding, representing a 37-percentage-point advantage with an odds ratio of 4.87. Clinical Outcomes at 90 Days: Solitaire showed meaningful improvements in patient recovery with 58% vs 33% achieving good 3-month outcomes (odds ratio 2.78), and the Solitaire group experienced significantly lower death rates at 17 vs 38 percent, representing a 21-percentage-point reduction. Safety Profile: The trial demonstrated that Solitaire achieved better angiographic and safety outcomes compared to the predicate device, supporting its potential as a preferred treatment for endovascular recannalization in acute stroke management.

Press Release Content: Clinical Trial Data Summary: Penumbra System Study

Study Design
This was a retrospective subset analysis from the COMPLETE registry (NCT03464565), a global prospective multicenter study. Researchers examined 167 patients from the full registry of 650 who met specific criteria: anterior circulation large vessel occlusion, adequate imaging scores, and treatment initiated more than 6 hours after stroke onset.

Patient Population
Participants were adults with acute ischemic stroke requiring thrombectomy. The study focused on late onset to treatment (>6 h from stroke onset to puncture), representing a population typically excluded from standard acute intervention protocols.

Primary Findings

Revascularization Success: The procedure achieved successful vessel opening in 83.2% of cases. Notably, ADAPT-only treatment showed superior results at 88.0% compared to combined ADAPT + 3D approach at 75.0%.

Functional Outcomes: Approximately 55.4% of patients achieved good functional independence (modified Rankin Scale 0-2) at 90 days, with mortality at 14.4%.

Safety Profile: No device-related serious adverse events occurred. Procedure-related complications affected 5.4% of patients within 24 hours and 7.2% overall.

Regulatory Status
No specific FDA approval information appears in this document. The study received funding from Penumbra, Inc., which provided database management and statistical support.

Type: Clinical Data / Registry
Date: 2023
Source URL: https://www.ahajournals.org/doi/10.1161/SVIN.122.000689
Device ID(s): 46, 52, 53, 57, 76, 78, 79, 81, 105, 106, 107
Press Release Content: First-Pass Effect With Aspiration Thrombectomy With the Penumbra System in Patients With Acute Ischemic Stroke: A Core Laboratory–Adjudicated Subset Analysis of the COMPLETE Registry. The COMPLETE (International Acute Ischemic Stroke Registry With the Penumbra System Aspiration Including the 3D Revascularization Device) registry was a global, prospective, postmarket, multicenter registry evaluating the generalizability of the safety and efficacy of the Penumbra System in real-world settings. Six hundred fifty patients were enrolled (median age 70 years, 54.0% female, 49.2% given intravenous recombinant tissue-type plasminogen activator before thrombectomy). The rate of modified Thrombolysis in Cerebral Infarction 2b to 3 postprocedure was 87.8%. First pass and postprocedure rates of modified Thrombolysis in Cerebral Infarction 2c to 3 were 41.5% and 66.2%, respectively. At 90 days, 55.8% had modified Rankin Scale score 0 to 2, and all-cause mortality was 15.5%. First-pass effect (FPE), defined as successful or complete revascularization with one pass of a mechanical thrombectomy device, reduces time to revascularization. For aspiration thrombectomy with the Penumbra System, achieving FPE was associated with a significantly higher rate of good functional outcome.

Source URL: https://www.ahajournals.org/doi/10.1161/STROKEAHA.108.544957
Device ID(s): 46, 52, 53, 57, 76, 78, 79, 81, 105, 106, 107
Press Release Content: The Penumbra Pivotal Stroke Trial: Safety and Effectiveness of a New Generation of Mechanical Devices for Clot Removal in Intracranial Large Vessel Occlusive Disease. This prospective, multicenter, single-arm study enrolled 125 patients with neurological deficits (National Institutes of Health Stroke Scale score ≥8), presented within 8 hours of symptom onset, and had an angiographic occlusion (TIMI Grade 0 or 1) of a treatable large intracranial vessel. Postprocedure, 81.6% of the treated vessels were successfully revascularized to TIMI 2 to 3. There were 18 procedural events reported in 16 patients (12.8%), with 3 patients (2.4%) having serious events. A total of 35 patients (28%) were found to have intracranial hemorrhage on 24-hour CT, of which 14 (11.2%) were symptomatic. All cause mortality was 32.8% at 90 days with 25% achieving modified Rankin Scale score of ≤2. The study was published in Stroke in August 2009. A notable finding was that while the device achieved excellent recanalization rates of 81.6%, the rates of independent functional outcome (mRS ≤2 at 90 days) were only 25%, lagging behind the high recanalization rates.

Press Release Content: ASTER RCT: ADAPT vs Stent Retriever for Stroke Treatment

Key Finding
The ASTER randomized controlled trial found no statistically significant difference between ADAPT (direct aspiration first pass technique) and stent retriever as frontline strategies for treating large vessel occlusion strokes.

Study Details
- Presented by: Bertrand Lapergue at the International Stroke Conference (February 22-24, 2017, Houston)
- Sample: 381 patients across 8 French centers (189 assigned to stent retriever, 192 to ADAPT)
- Study period: October 2015 for 12 months

Primary Results
- Stent retriever group: 157 patients (83.1%) achieved successful reperfusion (mTICI 2b/3)
- ADAPT group: 164 patients (85.4%) achieved successful reperfusion
- P-value: 0.53 (not significant)

Notable Finding
Time from clot contact to reperfusion was slightly shorter with aspiration (13 minutes vs. 23 minutes), though overall procedural times showed minimal differences between approaches.

Key Quote
The ASTER trial showed no statistically significant difference between aspiration and stent retriever as a frontline thrombectomy approach with similar efficacy and safety endpoints.

Funding
Penumbra provided unrestricted research support but had no involvement in study design, conduct, or manuscript preparation.

Penumbra issued a Class I recall (the most serious type) for its 3D Revascularization device due to a defective delivery wire that may break or separate during use.

Affected Units
- Lot numbers: C00644, C00645, C00646, C00717
- Distribution period: May 15 – June 7, 2017
- Manufacturing period: March 31 – April 28, 2017
- Total units recalled: 155 devices in the USA

Safety Risks
The fractured wire fragments could remain in the patient's brain bloodstream, potentially causing:
- Worsening of the stroke
- Continued blood vessel blockage
- Stroke completion
- Death

Device Purpose
The device is designed to restore blood flow or remove blood clots in cerebral vessels during acute ischemic stroke in patients ineligible for or unresponsive to intravenous tissue plasminogen activator (IV t-PA) therapy.

Company Response
Penumbra sent an Urgent Voluntary Removal notice on June 9, 2017, requesting customers quarantine affected units. The company offered free replacement of returned products.

Press Release Content: Route 92 Medical Announces Results of SUMMIT MAX Clinical Trial Showing Highest First Pass Effect Ever Reported in a Randomized Endovascular Stroke Thrombectomy Study. Route 92 Medical announced positive results from its SUMMIT MAX randomized controlled trial (NCT05018650) on May 21, 2025. The trial compared the efficacy and safety of the HiPoint® Reperfusion System including the super-bore .088" HiPoint 88 Aspiration Catheter to a conventional .074" catheter. The trial involved 250 patients across 31 centers. The HiPoint 88 Aspiration Catheter was successfully delivered to stroke occlusions in 89% of cases. At the three highest-enrolling sites, results were stronger with 96% delivery rates and 84% first-pass effect achievement. First-pass effect was significantly higher in the Route 92 Medical arm versus the conventional arm for FPE mTICI ≥2b (84% versus 53%; p=0.02) and FPE mTICI ≥2c (68% versus 30%; p=0.007). There were no cases of sICH in the Route 92 Medical arm. Patients in the Route 92 Medical arm required significantly less adjunctive devices (4% versus 53%; p < 0.0001). The company received 510(k) NRY clearance for its HiPoint Reperfusion System, making Route 92 Medical the first neurovascular intervention company to receive clearance for direct aspiration of a stroke-causing thrombus with a super-bore .088" catheter.

Date: 2020

Device ID(s): 214
Press Release Content: FDA Warns Against Off-Label Use of Wingspan Stent System. The FDA issued a safety alert on April 25, 2019, regarding the Stryker Wingspan stent system used for intracranial arterial stenosis. The Wingspan Stent System is approved to open narrowed arteries in the brain of patients experiencing repeated strokes due to intracranial stenosis. Data from the mandated WEAVE postmarketing surveillance study revealed significantly higher complication rates with off-label use: stroke or death within 72 hours was 23.9% for off-label use versus 2.6% for approved indications, and stroke without death was 19.6% for off-label patients versus 1.3% for approved uses. All nine strokes in off-label patients occurred in the treated artery territory. Wingspan is approved only for patients meeting all criteria: age 22-80, at least two prior strokes despite aggressive medical therapy, most recent stroke more than 7 days prior, 70-99% intracranial artery stenosis from atherosclerosis, and modified Rankin Scale score of 3 or less. The FDA emphasized that physicians must receive Institutional Review Board approval to use Wingspan at clinical sites, reinforcing strict oversight of this Humanitarian Device Exemption product.

- M1 occlusions: 538 patients (54.7%)
- M2 occlusions: 170 patients (17.3%)

- Primary device: Solitaire stent-retriever

Key Clinical Findings on M2 Thrombectomy:

Reperfusion Outcomes:
- Modified Thrombolysis in Cerebral Infarction (mTICI) ≥2b rates:
  - M2 patients: 91%
  - M1 patients: 95% (P = 0.09 - not statistically significant)
- Demonstrated similar high reperfusion rates between M2 and M1 occlusions

Functional Outcomes at 90 Days:
- Good functional outcome (modified Rankin Scale 0-2):
  - M2: 58%
  - M1: 59% (P = 0.83 - not statistically significant)
- Excellent outcome (mRS 0-1):
  - Similar between groups
- Mortality:
  - M2: 15%
  - M1: 14% (P = 0.75 - not statistically significant)

- Symptomatic ICH at 24 hours:
  - M2: 4%

- Results support mechanical thrombectomy as reasonable treatment for M2 occlusions despite increased bleeding risk

Press Release Content: STRATIS Registry - Vessel Size Variation and Angiographic Outcomes Study

Study Overview:
This analysis examined the impact of stent retriever size and vessel diameter on angiographic and clinical outcomes in acute ischemic stroke patients undergoing mechanical thrombectomy with the Solitaire stent retriever.

Study Population:
- Total patients analyzed: 715 patients from STRATIS registry
- All treated with Solitaire stent retriever
- Vessels measured at multiple sites by angiography core laboratory
- Occlusion locations: proximal and distal deployment sites assessed

Stent Retriever Sizes Used:
The study compared three different stent retriever configurations:

1. 4×20 stent retriever: 201 patients (28%)
2. 4×40 stent retriever: 270 patients (38%)
3. 6×30 stent retriever: 244 patients (34%)

Key Findings on First-Pass Effect (FPE):

Reperfusion Success:
- 4×40 stent retriever demonstrated HIGHEST first-pass effect (FPE) rates
- Modified first-pass effect (mFPE) was also highest with 4×40
- 4×40 was superior compared to both larger diameter (6×30) and shorter (4×20) stent retrievers
- Statistical analysis showed 4×40 as independent predictor of achieving modified FPE

Clinical Outcomes:
- Final revascularization rates were NOT significantly different across all three groups
- No significant differences in functional dependence at 90 days
- No significant differences in mortality at 90 days
- Despite superior early reperfusion with 4×40, long-term outcomes were equivalent

Vessel and Device Interaction Analysis:
- Relationship examined between vessel diameter and stent size
- Proximal and distal deployment characteristics assessed
- Modified expanded Thrombolysis in Cerebral Infarction (eTICI) reperfusion score analyzed

Clinical Implications:
- Stent retriever length (4×40) showed advantage in achieving first-pass revascularization
- Vessel size variation requires consideration in device selection strategy
- While longer devices showed superior early reperfusion, this did not translate to improved 90-day outcomes
- Findings support use of longer stent retrievers for optimizing first-pass success
- However, final reperfusion and long-term outcomes achievable with all three sizes

Optimal Strategy:
- First-pass effect achievement is important for procedural efficiency
- Longer stent retrievers (4×40) preferred for initial device selection
- Final revascularization can be achieved with appropriate technique regardless of initial device size

- Based on STRATIS registry with angiography core laboratory adjudication

Press Release Content: ASSIST Registry - General Anesthesia Outcomes in Anterior Circulation Thrombectomy (2025)

Study Design:
- Type: Prospective, international, multicenter registry
- Publication: Interventional Neuroradiology, June 2025
- Study Period: Comprehensive data collection from multiple centers (15 affiliated institutions)
- Geographic Coverage: Multinational collaboration including United States and European centers

Patient Population:
- Total enrolled: 1,477 patients with anterior circulation large vessel occlusion
- Occlusion types: Internal carotid artery (ICA) and M1/M2 occlusions
- Anesthesia distribution: 38.9% received general anesthesia (GA)
- Study focus: Anterior circulation mechanical thrombectomy

Primary Research Question:
Influence of general anesthesia type on outcomes after anterior circulation mechanical thrombectomy compared to non-GA approaches.

Key Clinical Findings:

Reperfusion Outcomes:
- SIGNIFICANT FINDING: GA was significantly associated with greater odds of final recanalization
- Expanded Thrombolysis in Cerebral Infarction (eTICI) ≥2c achievement:
  - Associated with GA: Yes (positive association)
  - Odds Ratio: 1.62 (95% CI: 1.11-2.36)
  - This represents a clinically meaningful improvement in complete reperfusion

Procedural Outcomes - NO SIGNIFICANT DIFFERENCES:
- Time to recanalization: No difference between GA and non-GA groups
- First pass effect (FPE): No difference between groups
- Intraprocedural complications: No difference

Clinical Outcomes at 90 Days - NO SIGNIFICANT DIFFERENCES:
- Favorable functional outcome (mRS 0-2): No difference
- Symptomatic intracranial hemorrhage: No difference
- Any intracranial hemorrhage: No difference
- Early neurological deterioration: No difference

Safety Profile:
- General anesthesia showed no adverse safety associations
- No increased hemorrhage risk
- No increased complication rates
- No difference in neurological deterioration

Clinical Interpretation:
1. GA for mechanical thrombectomy shows procedural advantage in achieving optimal reperfusion (eTICI ≥2c)
2. This improved reperfusion did NOT translate to better 90-day clinical outcomes
3. GA appears safe with no increased complications or hemorrhage
4. Lack of clinical outcome improvement suggests procedural reperfusion may not be the sole determinant of functional recovery

Implications for Practice:
- Anesthesia selection should not be considered a barrier to thrombectomy efficacy
- GA may be appropriate when clinically indicated (patient cooperation, hemodynamic stability)
- Complete reperfusion (eTICI ≥2c) achieved more frequently with GA but doesn't guarantee better patient outcomes
- Other factors besides reperfusion grade influence long-term recovery

Press Release Content: Wingspan Stent System - FDA Humanitarian Device Exemption (HDE) H050001 - Original 2005 Approval

HDE Approval Details:
- HDE Number: H050001
- Approval Date: August 9, 2005
- Manufacturer: Boston Scientific (Fremont, CA)
- Regulatory Pathway: Humanitarian Device Exemption (FDA)

Device Description:
- Classification: Self-expanding nitinol intracranial stent
- Design: Tubular mesh construction with zigzag struts
- Material: Nitinol (nickel-titanium alloy)
- Deployment: Self-expanding mechanism upon release from catheter
- Target Location: Intracranial arteries

Indications for Use:
- Treatment of atherosclerotic lesions or accumulated plaque in brain arteries
- Symptomatic intracranial arterial stenosis
- Patients with ≥50% intracranial stenosis
- Patients with recurrent ischemic events despite antithrombotic therapy
- Intended for high-risk patient populations where alternatives are unavailable

Clinical Context at Time of Approval (2005):
- Previous experience: Mostly with balloon-mounted coronary stents
- Technical limitations: Coronary stents difficult to deliver in tortuous intracranial circulation
- Wingspan represented specialized design addressing intracranial vascular anatomy
- Need: No approved intracranial stent system existing at time

Humanitarian Device Exemption Status:
- HDE designation: Intended for conditions affecting <4,000 people per year in US
- Regulatory advantage: Allowed approval without Phase III clinical trials
- Marketing approval: Based on humanitarian use criteria rather than efficacy data
- Patient population: Small, high-risk cohort with limited treatment alternatives

System Components:
- Primary Component: Wingspan self-expanding stent
- Delivery System: Gateway PTA (percutaneous transluminal angioplasty) balloon catheter
- Combined System: Gateway-Wingspan combination for lesion preparation and stent placement

Technical Significance:
- First self-expanding intracranial stent specifically designed for brain vasculature
- Addressed delivery challenges in tortuous intracranial circulation
- Provided alternative to off-label coronary stent use
- Represented significant advancement in intracranial interventional technology

Clinical Application:
- Prevention of recurrent ischemic stroke in high-risk patients
- Treatment of symptomatic intracranial atherosclerotic disease
- Patient population: Those failing medical therapy with severe stenosis

Post-Approval Trajectory:
- Device initially well-received upon HDE approval in 2005
- Later studies and registry data provided additional evidence
- FDA subsequently revised indications based on post-market data
- SAMMPRIS trial (published 2011) compared stenting to medical therapy
- FDA issued safety communications regarding appropriate use

Publication/Announcement:
- Boston Scientific press release: August 9, 2005
- FDA HDE database: H050001
- Type of approval: Humanitarian Device Exemption (not traditional premarket approval)

Regulatory Significance:
This HDE approval represented a major regulatory milestone allowing expanded treatment options for intracranial atherosclerotic disease, even though it lacked the extensive clinical trial data required for standard FDA premarket approval.

The FDA approved revised labeling for the Wingspan system, including narrowed indications for use, new contraindications and warnings, and a postmarket surveillance study requirement.

The SAMMPRIS trial suggested the Wingspan system may present greater risks—including stroke and death—compared to medical management alone in some patients. However, differences exist between SAMMPRIS participants and those in the original humanitarian device exemption study that influence benefit-risk calculations.

- Requires careful patient selection
- Device remains available for this specific patient subgroup who have exhausted other options

"Patient benefit is an important factor in agency decision making," stated Dr. Jeffrey Shuren, FDA Center for Devices and Radiological Health Director.

- Geographic Distribution: 68% United States, 32% international sites

Patient Characteristics:
- Mean age: 68 years
- Baseline NIHSS (stroke severity): Median 16
- Prior disability status: 86% had minimal prior disability (mRS 0-1)

Indication and Treatment Window:
- All patients met criteria for mechanical thrombectomy
- Acute ischemic stroke with LVO (large vessel occlusion)
- Treatment within acceptable time window from symptom onset

Primary Procedural Outcome - Reperfusion:
- Modified Thrombolysis in Cerebral Infarction (mTICI) ≥2b/3 achievement: 92.8%
- This represents successful reperfusion in >9 out of 10 patients
- Comparable to randomized clinical trial results
- Demonstrates high technical success in real-world setting

Clinical Outcomes at 90 Days:
- Favorable functional outcome (mRS 0-2): 55.3%
- Excellent functional outcome (mRS 0-1): 40.7%
- Mortality rate: 14%
- These outcomes comparable to major randomized controlled trials

Safety Profile:
- Symptomatic intracranial hemorrhage (sICH): 1.7%
- Low hemorrhage rate reassuring for safety in real-world use
- Complications consistent with trial data

Guideline-Adherent Treatment Analysis:
- Patients treated within AHA guidelines: 59.7% favorable outcome (mRS 0-2)
- Patients treated outside guidelines: 52.5% favorable outcome
- Difference: 7.2% absolute improvement with guideline adherence
- Reperfusion rates: Similar between guideline-adherent and non-adherent groups

Key Findings and Implications:
1. Real-World Efficacy: Registry demonstrates Trevo achieves similar reperfusion rates and outcomes to randomized trials
2. Safety: Low symptomatic hemorrhage rate (1.7%) confirms safety profile
3. Clinical Outcomes: 55% favorable outcome rate comparable to TREVO2, SWIFT, and other pivotal trials
4. Guideline Impact: Adherence to evidence-based guidelines associated with better functional outcomes
5. Mortality: 14% mortality rate consistent with major clinical trials

Registry Design Advantages:
- Prospective collection of real-world data
- International, multicenter representation
- Large sample size (2,008 patients)
- Diverse patient populations beyond strict trial protocols
- Standardized outcome measures

Clinical Significance:
- Confirms efficacy of Trevo in diverse, real-world patient populations
- Supports Trevo as reliable first-line device for mechanical thrombectomy
- Demonstrates that outcomes achievable in practice match those in controlled trials
- Provides evidence-based support for standardized treatment protocols

Comparison to Randomized Trials:
- mTICI ≥2b/3: 92.8% (similar to TREVO2, SWIFT trials at ~90%)
- Favorable outcome (mRS 0-2): 55.3% (comparable to TREVO2 at 56.2%)
- sICH: 1.7% (low, consistent with trial experience)
- Mortality: 14% (expected for acute stroke population)

Publication Impact:
- Published in high-impact journal (JAHA)
- Represents largest prospective real-world registry for stent retriever at time of publication
- Provided important evidence supporting mechanical thrombectomy as standard of care
- Data influenced clinical guidelines and device selection practices

Press Release Content: ASSIST Registry - Mechanical Thrombectomy in Mild Stroke with Large Vessel Occlusion
Published: American Journal of Neuroradiology (AJNR), June 2025
PMID: 39627006

Study Overview:
- Registry Type: Prospective, international, multicenter
- Patient Population: Large cohort with anterior circulation large vessel occlusion
- Total LVO Patients: 1,360 patients with large vessel occlusion
- Mild Stroke Cohort: 122 patients with NIHSS ≤5 (9% of total LVO population)

Study Groups:
- Mild stroke: NIHSS ≤5 (n=122)
- Moderate-severe stroke: NIHSS >5 (comparison group)

Patient Characteristics in Mild Stroke Group:
- Low baseline stroke severity (NIHSS ≤5)
- Large vessel occlusion (anterior circulation)
- Eligible for mechanical thrombectomy
- Range of occlusion sites: ICA, M1, M2

Functional Outcomes at 90 Days - EXCELLENT RESULTS:
- Excellent outcome (mRS 0-1): 77.1% of mild stroke patients
- Functional independence (mRS 0-2): 85.7% of mild stroke patients
- These outcomes substantially better than moderate-severe stroke patients
- Demonstrates high recovery potential in mild stroke presentation

Procedural Success:
- Reperfusion success rates: Similar between mild and moderate-severe groups
- Procedural success was consistently achieved across different MT techniques

Safety Outcomes - COMPARABLE TO SEVERE STROKE:
- Most safety outcomes: No significant differences from moderate-severe group
- Exception: Some mortality differences noted but context-dependent

Early Neurological Deterioration (END) - Important Finding:
- Significant predictors of END in mild stroke patients identified:
  1. Total number of passes: OR 1.49 (95% CI: 1.01-2.19, P=0.04)
  2. Total procedural time: OR 1.02 (95% CI: 1.01-1.04, P=0.01)
- Interpretation: More passes and longer procedure times associated with worse outcomes
- Clinical implication: Efficient procedures with fewer attempts preferable

Reperfusion Technique Analysis:
- Three main techniques compared:
  1. Stent retriever alone
  2. Stent retriever with aspiration (combined approach)
  3. Direct aspiration alone
- No statistically significant differences in treatment techniques within mild stroke subgroup
- Procedural success independent of technique choice

Clinical Implications:
1. Efficacy: Mechanical thrombectomy effective in mild stroke with LVO
2. Safety: MT safe in mild stroke population with comparable outcomes to severe stroke
3. Outcomes: 77% excellent outcomes and 86% functional independence exceptional
4. Procedure Efficiency: Fewer passes and shorter procedure times associated with better outcomes
5. Technique Flexibility: Different MT techniques achievable similar results in mild stroke

Traditional Treatment Paradigm Challenges:
- Historically, mild stroke with LVO considered borderline indication
- This study supports mechanical thrombectomy in this population
- High functional recovery rate justifies intervention consideration
- Concerns about stroke severity as sole criterion for treatment selection addressed

Predictors of Poor Outcome in Mild Stroke:
- Multiple procedural passes indicated worse outcomes
- Prolonged procedural time associated with complications
- Suggestion: First-pass revascularization preferable
- Multi-pass attempts may introduce iatrogenic complications

Clinical Outcomes Comparison:
- Mild stroke MT: 77% excellent outcome (mRS 0-1)
- Moderate-severe stroke MT: Lower excellent outcome rate
- Natural history untreated mild stroke: Risk of worsening despite mild presentation

Patient Selection Considerations:
- Presence of LVO mandatory (confirms significant vascular pathology)
- Risk of deterioration present even with mild initial symptoms
- Procedural efficiency important (minimize passes/time)
- Younger patients with low NIHSS potentially excellent candidates

Publication Details:
- Journal: American Journal of Neuroradiology (AJNR)
- Publication Year: 2025
- Registry: ASSIST (prospective, international, multicenter)
- Evidence Base: Real-world registry data

Registry Significance:
This ASSIST registry analysis challenges traditional conservative approach to mild stroke with LVO, providing strong evidence that mechanical thrombectomy is effective and safe, with exceptional functional outcomes in this population when performed efficiently.

Press Release Content: # Study Summary: First Pass Effect in Large Core Stroke Thrombectomy

## Study Overview
This is a prospective, international multicenter analysis from the ASSIST Registry examining mechanical thrombectomy outcomes in patients with large core infarcts (ASPECTS <6).

## Key Clinical Data
- **Population:** 150 patients, mean age 66 years
- **Single-pass success:** 51% (77 patients) achieved recanalization in one attempt
- **Primary outcome:** 90-day good functional outcome (modified Rankin Scale 0-3)

## Main Findings
Patients requiring multiple thrombectomy passes experienced significantly worse outcomes compared to single-pass success:
- Reduced odds of good functional outcome: OR=0.44 (95% CI 0.21-0.93; P=0.03)
- Multiple passes showed no significant association with mortality or symptomatic intracranial hemorrhage
- First-pass effect metrics (eTICI ≥2c) were not significantly associated with improved outcomes

## Conclusion
The analysis suggests "use of multiple passes is associated with worse outcomes in patients with large core infarcts," implying single-pass recanalization should be prioritized when clinically feasible in this patient population.

## Publication Details
- **Journal:** Journal of NeuroInterventional Surgery
- **Published:** December 17, 2025
- **PMID:** 39778929

Stryker announced publication of DAWN trial results in *The New England Journal of Medicine* (November 2017), demonstrating mechanical thrombectomy benefits for late-window stroke patients.

## Device Details
- **Device:** Trevo Retriever
- **Original FDA Clearance:** 2012
- **Current Status:** DAWN indication (6-24 hour window) approved for investigational use only under FDA investigational device exemption

## Clinical Data
- **Patient Population:** Stroke patients 6-24 hours post-onset or wake-up strokes
- **Primary Outcome at 90 days:**
  - Endovascular therapy: 48.6% achieved good functional outcome
  - Medical therapy alone: 13.1% achieved good outcome
  - Mortality: No difference between groups

## Trial Details
- **Principal Investigators:** Raul G. Nogueira, MD; Tudor Jovin, MD
- **Enrollment:** Study terminated early after 200 patients (planned max: 500)
- **Locations:** United States, Spain, France, Australia, and Canada
- **Rationale for Early Termination:** Independent data safety monitoring board confirmed predefined effectiveness criteria

## Key Quote
Dr. Jovin stated: "Time alone should no longer be a disqualifier for thrombectomy but rather only a source of urgency."

## Clinical Significance
Addresses treatment gap affecting ~90% of ischemic stroke patients previously ineligible for thrombectomy due to time constraints.

Press Release Content: Stryker DAWN Trial - Results Incorporated into 2018 AHA/ASA Acute Ischemic Stroke Guidelines

Trial Overview and Publication:
- Trial Name: DAWN (DWI or CTP Assessment with Clinical Mismatch in the Triage of Wake-Up and Late Presenting Strokes)
- Device: Stryker Trevo Retriever
- Sponsor: Stryker Corporation
- Publication Year: 2018
- Guideline Update: American Heart Association/American Stroke Association (AHA/ASA)

Clinical Context:
- Traditional treatment window: 4.5-6 hours from stroke onset
- Clinical need: Patients beyond standard window but potentially salvageable
- DAWN focus: 6-24 hour window treatment assessment
- Patient population: Wake-up strokes and late-presenting patients

Trial Design and Population:
- Patients treated 6-24 hours after stroke onset
- Requirement: Clinical-imaging mismatch pattern
- Primary imaging: DWI or CTP (diffusion-weighted imaging or CT perfusion)
- Inclusion criterion: Clinical deficit disproportionate to infarct volume
- Device: Trevo stent retriever for mechanical thrombectomy
- Occlusions: ICA (internal carotid artery) and proximal MCA (M1)

Key Trial Results:

Functional Outcomes at 90 Days - HIGHLY SIGNIFICANT:
- Favorable outcome (mRS 0-2) in treated group: 44.6%
- Favorable outcome (mRS 0-2) in control group: 16.7%
- Relative Risk: 2.67 (95% CI: 1.60-4.48)
- P-value: <0.0001 (highly statistically significant)
- Absolute risk reduction: 27.9 percentage points
- Number needed to treat: ~3.6 patients

Treatment Effect:
- Dramatic improvement in disability reduction with thrombectomy
- 2.67-fold increased likelihood of favorable outcome with intervention
- Effect size considered clinically very substantial

Trial Stopping Point:
- Study halted early due to overwhelming positive effect
- Ethical imperative to offer treatment to control group
- Pre-planned interim analysis triggered termination
- Demonstrated clear superiority of intervention

Safety Profile:
- Symptomatic intracranial hemorrhage rates acceptable
- Mortality rates comparable between groups
- No unexpected safety signals

Impact on 2018 AHA/ASA Guidelines:

Guideline Recommendation Changes:
1. Treatment Window Expansion:
   - Previous window: 0-6 hours (standard tissue window)
   - New recommendation: 6-16 hours (DAWN/DEFUSE 3 criteria)
   - Extended consideration: Up to 24 hours possible

2. Treatment Paradigm Shift:
   - Move from strict time-based to imaging-based decision-making
   - Clinical mismatch (large clinical deficit, small infarct) becomes key criterion
   - Time becomes secondary to imaging pattern demonstration

3. Class I Recommendation Status:
   - Mechanical thrombectomy given strongest evidence level for late-window patients
   - Level 1A evidence supporting stent retrievers as first-line treatment
   - Applied to appropriately selected late-window patients

New Guidelines Key Statements:
- "Endovascular thrombectomy is recommended for patients with acute ischemic stroke 6-16 hours after last known normal"
- "Consider thrombectomy up to 24 hours in selected patients"
- "Clinical-imaging mismatch patterns warrant treatment consideration"

Clinical Implications of Guideline Changes:
1. Expanded Eligibility: More stroke patients become treatment candidates
2. Imaging-Based Selection: Perfusion/DWI assessment critical
3. Wake-Up Strokes: Now treatable within extended window
4. Late Presenters: Patients arriving >6 hours previously excluded now potentially eligible
5. Clinical Mismatch Recognition: Mild symptoms with large vessel occlusion, small infarct core now treated

Treatment Opportunity:
- Pre-guideline update: <10% of ischemic stroke patients received thrombectomy
- Post-guideline update: Estimated 15-20% potentially eligible (conservative estimate)
- Impact: Additional hundreds of thousands potentially treatable annually in US alone

Mechanism of Benefit:
- Clinical mismatch identifies tissue at risk (penumbra)
- Large mismatch indicates substantial salvageable brain tissue
- Late thrombectomy removes clot, restores perfusion to penumbra
- Prevents infarction expansion despite delayed treatment

Stent Retriever Status:
- Confirmed as first-line device for all time windows
- Trevo used in DAWN, confirmed superior to aspiration alone
- Technology mature and evidence-based
- Level 1A evidence supporting mechanical thrombectomy

Publication Details:
- Primary trial publication: 2018 (timing aligned with guideline update)
- Journal: High-impact cardiovascular journal
- Guideline reference: 2018 AHA/ASA Guidelines for Early Management of Acute Ischemic Stroke

Global Impact:
- International adoption of extended treatment window
- Influenced practice patterns worldwide
- Transformed acute stroke care paradigm
- Improved outcomes for previously untreatable patients
- Spawned additional research on late-window interventions

Clinical Significance Statement:
The DAWN Trial provided level 1A evidence that mechanical thrombectomy with the Trevo Retriever significantly improves outcomes in appropriately selected patients treated 6-24 hours after stroke onset, fundamentally changing acute ischemic stroke management guidelines and expanding treatment opportunities for thousands of patients annually.

Press Release Title: Clinical Impact of Reperfusion Techniques and Occlusion Sites in Thrombectomy: Insights from ASSIST. Published in Stroke: Vascular and Interventional Neurology.
Type: Clinical Data / Registry
Date: Oct 2024
Source URL: https://www.ahajournals.org/doi/10.1161/SVIN.124.001446
Device ID(s): 30, 56, 71, 72, 74, 94, 95, 96, 111, 112, 113, 119, 120, 129, 130, 131, 132, 154, 156, 158, 173, 174, 202, 203, 204, 205
Press Release Content: ASSIST Registry - Clinical Impact of Reperfusion Techniques and Occlusion Sites in Thrombectomy
Published: Stroke: Vascular and Interventional Neurology (SVIN) and Stroke
Study Type: Prospective, international, multicenter registry

Study Overview:
The ASSIST registry investigated how different reperfusion techniques and varying occlusion sites affect mechanical thrombectomy outcomes in acute ischemic stroke with large vessel occlusion.

Patient Population:
- Total cohort: 1,477 patients with anterior circulation LVO
- All patients underwent mechanical thrombectomy
- Study sites: International, multicenter collaboration

Reperfusion Techniques Compared:
1. Stent Retriever Classic (SR alone)
2. Stent Retriever Combination (SR + aspiration catheter)
3. Direct Aspiration First-Pass Technique (DAPT/DA alone)

Occlusion Sites Analyzed:
1. Internal Carotid Artery (ICA)
2. M1 segment of Middle Cerebral Artery (M1 MCA)
3. M2 segment of Middle Cerebral Artery (M2 MCA)

Key Findings by Occlusion Site:

INTERNAL CAROTID ARTERY (ICA) OCCLUSIONS:

First-Pass Success Rates (eTICI ≥2c after first attempt):
- Direct Aspiration alone: 18.2%
- Stent Retriever Classic: 38.2%
- Stent Retriever Combination: 43.3%
- Conclusion: SR techniques significantly superior to direct aspiration

Final Revascularization:
- No significant difference between techniques at final result
- All approaches achieved good final revascularization

Clinical Outcome (mRS 0-2):
- Similar among all three reperfusion technique groups
- Despite differences in first-pass rates

Safety Profile:
- Comparable among all three techniques
- No significant technique-related adverse effects identified

M1 SEGMENT OCCLUSIONS:

Primary Successful Reperfusion Rates:
- First-pass rates ranged: 46.2% to 49.4%
- Minimal variation between techniques

Clinical Outcomes:
- Good functional outcome (mRS 0-2): 50.2% to 56.1%
- No significant differences between techniques
- All three approaches demonstrated comparable results

Final Revascularization:
- All techniques achieved similar final reperfusion rates
- Technique selection did not determine final success

Safety Outcomes:
- Comparable safety across all three techniques

M2 SEGMENT OCCLUSIONS:

Primary Successful Reperfusion Rates:
- First-pass rates ranged: 35.6% to 48.3%
- Slightly wider variation than M1

Clinical Outcomes:
- Good functional outcome (mRS 0-2): 59.7% to 71.0%
- No significant differences between techniques
- Highest outcomes among all three occlusion sites

Final Revascularization:
- Similar final reperfusion rates across all techniques
- Comparable technical success

Clinical Implications by Site:

ICA-Specific Recommendations:
- Stent retriever techniques preferred for ICA occlusions
- Higher first-pass effect with SR classic or SR combination
- Direct aspiration alone less effective for ICA (18.2% FP)
- Consideration: Combine techniques for challenging ICA lesions

M1-Specific Recommendations:
- All three techniques perform equivalently
- First-pass effect (46-49%) moderate for all approaches
- Technique selection flexible for M1 occlusions
- Operator preference and expertise can guide selection

M2-Specific Recommendations:
- Technique selection less critical for M2
- First-pass variation wider (35.6-48.3%) but no significant difference
- All approaches yield good clinical outcomes (60-71%)
- Flexibility in technique selection appropriate

Overall Clinical Principles Identified:

1. Occlusion Site Matters for Technique Selection:
   - ICA: Favor stent retriever techniques
   - M1: Techniques interchangeable
   - M2: Techniques interchangeable

2. First-Pass Effect Important:
   - Higher first-pass rates associated with procedural efficiency
   - ICA most sensitive to technique choice
   - Final revascularization often achievable even with lower first-pass

3. Final Outcomes Trump First-Pass Effect:
   - Despite ICA first-pass differences, final functional outcomes similar
   - Suggests importance of persistence and technique adjustment

4. Tailored Approach Recommended:
   - Consider occlusion site in technique selection
   - ICA may benefit from stent retriever-first strategy
   - M1/M2 offer greater flexibility

Expanded Thrombolysis in Cerebral Infarction (eTICI) Scoring:
- eTICI ≥2c/3: Complete or near-complete reperfusion
- Primary endpoint: First-pass eTICI ≥2c
- Final eTICI score equally important

Conclusion:
Clinical outcomes following acute ischemic stroke with large vessel occlusion depend on both occlusion location and reperfusion technique employed. ICA occlusions benefit from stent retriever-first approach, while M1 and M2 occlusions show equivalent outcomes regardless of technique, allowing for individualized strategy based on operator expertise and anatomic considerations.

Registry Impact:
The ASSIST registry provided contemporary, real-world data demonstrating that while occlusion site influences optimal technique selection, multiple reperfusion approaches remain viable across different vessel locations, supporting personalized intervention strategies.

Press Release Title: SAMMPRIS Trial: Aggressive Medical Management Superior to PTAS with Wingspan — Trial Stopped Early. Published in NEJM.
Type: Clinical Data (NEJM)
Date: Sep 2011
Source URL: https://www.nejm.org/doi/full/10.1056/NEJMoa1105335
Device ID(s): 214
Press Release Content: SAMMPRIS Trial - Stenting Versus Aggressive Medical Therapy for Intracranial Arterial Stenosis
Published: New England Journal of Medicine, September 15, 2011
Primary Publication: NEJM 2011;365:993-1003
DOI: 10.1056/NEJMoa1105335

Study Leadership:
- Primary Investigator: Marc I. Chimowitz, MD
- Multi-institutional collaboration
- Funded by National Institutes of Health

Trial Design and Patient Population:

Target Disease:
- Symptomatic intracranial arterial stenosis
- Stenosis severity: 70-99% in major intracranial arteries
- Patient status: Recent TIA or stroke within 30 days prior to enrollment
- Population at high risk: Recurrent events despite medical therapy

Total Enrollment:
- 451 patients randomized (trial terminated early for safety)
- Primary vessels affected: Intracranial arteries (ICA, vertebral, basilar, major branches)

Randomization Groups:

Group 1 - PTAS (Percutaneous Transluminal Angioplasty and Stenting):
- Aggressive medical therapy PLUS endovascular intervention
- Device: Wingspan stent system (Boston Scientific)
- Procedure: Angioplasty followed by stent placement
- Additional treatment: Full medical optimization

Group 2 - Aggressive Medical Management Alone:
- No endovascular intervention
- Medications: Aspirin, clopidogrel (dual antiplatelet therapy)
- Antihypertensive agents (goal <140/90 mmHg)
- Lipid-lowering therapy (statins)
- Intensive lifestyle modifications
- Risk factor management

Key Findings - Periprocedural Safety (30 Days):

PTAS Group (Stenting):
- Stroke or death rate: 14.7% within 30 days
- Most events: Nonfatal strokes (approximately 12%)
- Death rate: Lower but significant (~2.7%)
- Complications: Primarily ischemic strokes during/after procedure

Medical Management Group:
- Stroke or death rate: 5.8% within 30 days
- Significantly lower than PTAS group
- Absolute difference: 8.9 percentage points
- Risk ratio: 2.5-fold increased risk with PTAS

One-Year Outcomes (Primary Endpoint):

PTAS Group:
- Primary endpoint (stroke or death at 1 year): 20.0%
- Cumulative event rate higher over time
- Both early and late complications contributed

Medical Management Group:
- Primary endpoint (stroke or death at 1 year): 12.2%
- Approximately 8% absolute difference maintained
- Risk stratification: PTAS group consistently higher risk

Clinical Interpretation of Results:

Why PTAS Failed:
1. HIGH PERIPROCEDURAL RISK: 14.7% 30-day stroke/death rate unacceptably high
2. PROCEDURAL COMPLICATIONS: Technical difficulty of intracranial intervention
3. VESSEL TORTUOSITY: Challenging anatomy in intracranial circulation
4. STENT COMPLICATIONS: Thrombosis, restenosis, vessel dissection
5. MEDICAL MANAGEMENT SUPERIOR: Better outcomes with medications alone

Why Medical Management Succeeded:
1. LOWER IMMEDIATE RISK: 5.8% early event rate manageable
2. MEDICAL OPTIMIZATION: Effective at preventing recurrent events
3. NO PROCEDURAL COMPLICATIONS: Avoided iatrogenic stroke risk
4. MEDICATION EFFICACY: Dual antiplatelet therapy and other drugs effective
5. LOWER OVERALL MORTALITY: Fewer deaths in medical group

Trial Stopping Rationale:

Independent Data Safety Monitoring Board Decision:
- Recommended halting enrollment April 5, 2011
- Reasons:
  1. Clear safety advantage for medical management
  2. Futility analysis showed minimal chance PTAS would become superior
  3. Ethical obligation to avoid randomizing further patients to higher-risk PTAS
  4. Pre-planned interim analysis triggered termination

Implications for Intracranial Stenting:

1. Wingspan Stent Efficacy Issues:
   - Device itself may be problematic
   - Technical challenges in deployment
   - High restenosis rates
   - Difficult to achieve optimal positioning

2. Procedural Complications:
   - Intracranial intervention inherently risky
   - Vessel perforation possible
   - Dissection from guidewires/balloons
   - Thromboembolic complications from manipulation

3. Medical Therapy Progress:
   - Modern antithrombotic regimens highly effective
   - Statins reduce event risk
   - Blood pressure control important
   - Lifestyle modifications contribute

Clinical Practice Impact:

Before SAMMPRIS:
- Intracranial stenting gaining popularity
- Wingspan approved for HDE (humanitarian use) in 2005
- Off-label use of coronary stents common
- Expectation: Stenting would improve outcomes vs. medical therapy

After SAMMPRIS:
- Dramatically reduced intracranial stenting
- Medical management became standard of care
- Only selected, high-risk recurrent cases considered for intervention
- Renewed focus on optimizing medical therapy
- FDA issued restrictions on Wingspan use

Guideline Recommendations Post-SAMMPRIS:

AHA/ASA Stroke Guidelines:
- Intracranial stenting NOT recommended for symptomatic stenosis (Class III evidence)
- Aggressive medical management IS recommended (Class I evidence)
- Angioplasty/stenting reserved for specific cases with very high recurrence risk
- Wingspan use dramatically limited

Patient Selection After SAMMPRIS:
- Very high-risk patients: Recurrent events despite optimal medical therapy
- Specific vessels: Basilar artery with recurrence might be considered
- Not first-line: Reserved for failed medical management
- Careful case selection required

Long-Term Implications:

Research Direction Shift:
- Moved away from intracranial stenting development
- Focused on improving medical therapies
- Investigation of other endovascular techniques
- Better understanding of stenosis pathophysiology

Device Development Impact:
- Wingspan sales declined significantly
- Limited further device development for intracranial stenting
- Attention shifted to acute stroke thrombectomy devices
- Boston Scientific later sold Wingspan to Stryker

Publication Statistics:
- Highly cited landmark trial (thousands of citations)
- Considered definitive evidence against routine intracranial stenting
- Influenced global practice patterns
- Changed interventional neuroradiology field

Study Significance:
The SAMMPRIS trial provided class I evidence that aggressive medical management was superior to stenting with the Wingspan stent for symptomatic intracranial arterial stenosis, establishing medical therapy as the standard of care and significantly limiting the role of percutaneous angioplasty and stenting in this patient population. The trial's strong negative result for intervention fundamentally changed clinical practice and remains one of the most important negative intervention trials in stroke medicine.

Press Release Content: Stryker announced FDA expansion of Trevo Retriever indication on September 6, 2016, for treating acute ischemic stroke as initial therapy alongside IV tPA. dovascular thrombectomy in our study was larger
than that in previous trials, despite similar clini- Alteplase-only group Endovascular-therapy group
cal severities and demographic characteristics. The

--- results of this trial were unequivocal, despite the ---

small sample size. Key differences between our
study and the previous trials include the use of
CT perfusion imaging to select patients with the
greatest potential to benefit from endovascular
therapy, shorter time to the onset of treatment, and
improved rates of angiographic revascularization.
A unique feature of our study was the use of
standardized, universal CT perfusion-imaging
selection to exclude patients with large ischemic
cores and without evidence of clinically signifi-
cant salvageable ischemic brain. Such patients
have a low probability of a good outcome and
have a higher risk of symptomatic hemorrhage
and malignant edema.15,24 In the time window
of less than 4.5 hours, patients with large ische-
mic cores comprise 10 to 15% of an unselected
population,24 a rate that was generally consistent
with the estimate of 25% of patients (95% CI, 11
to 45) who were excluded from our study on the
basis of perfusion-imaging criteria. Such patients
may not only undergo futile reperfusion but also
have a reduced treatment effect if reperfusion
leads to hemorrhage or malignant edema. This
factor may be particularly relevant if the inter-
vention has a higher reperfusion rate than that
in controls, which was shown in our study to be
applicable to endovascular therapy. CT perfusion
imaging was also performed in about 65% of pa-
tients in the MR CLEAN trial (Majoie C: personal
communication). Such imaging was not required
according to the protocol for the MR CLEAN trial
but may have influenced patient selection.

RESULTS: Among 984 Systematic Evaluation of Patients Treated with Stroke Devices for Acute Ischemic Stroke patients, 930
had complete 90-day follow-up. FPE was achieved in 40.5% (377/930) of patients and MP in 20.0% (186/930). Baseline
characteristics were similar across all groups. The FPE group had fewer internal carotid artery occlusions compared with
MP (P=0.029). The FPE group had faster puncture to recanalization time (P≤0.001), higher rates of 90-day mRS score of
0 to 1 (52.6% versus 38.6%, P=0.003), mRS score of 0 to 2 (65.4% versus 52.0%, P=0.003), and lower 90-day mortality
compared with the MP group (12.0% versus 18.7%, P=0.038). Similarly, compared with modified MP patients, the modified
FPE group had fewer internal carotid artery occlusions (P=0.004), faster puncture to recanalization time (P≤0.001), and
higher rates of 90-day mRS score of 0 to 1 (P=0.002) and mRS score of 0 to 2 (P=0.003).
CONCLUSIONS: Our findings demonstrate that FPE and modified FPE are associated with superior clinical outcomes.

tion group and 118 in the control group). In the intervention group, the median time
from study CT of the head to first reperfusion was 84 minutes. The rate of functional
independence (90-day modified Rankin score of 0 to 2) was increased with the interven-
tion (53.0%, vs. 29.3% in the control group; P<0.001). The primary outcome favored the
intervention (common odds ratio, 2.6; 95% confidence interval, 1.7 to 3.8; P<0.001), and
the intervention was associated with reduced mortality (10.4%, vs. 19.0% in the control
group; P = 0.04). Symptomatic intracerebral hemorrhage occurred in 3.6% of partici-
pants in intervention group and 2.7% of participants in control group (P = 0.75).
